newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein says IRA truce "difficult".
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein says IRA truce "difficult".

text.p: Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams held out little immediate hope on Sunday of new IRA truce demanded by Britain, Ireland and the United States to breathe new life into Northern Ireland peace talks.
Adams said in a statement issued after a week of tension over Protestant Orange Order parades that the surrender of arms held by his guerrilla allies "still remains a major difficulty".
He was responding to Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, who told Sinn Fein on Sunday:
"Let the IRA/Sinn Fein make their decision, the ball is in their court."

Adams was echoing the IRA position that "decommissioning" should take place at the end of talks on a settlement between pro-British Unionist and pro-Irish nationalists, not before or even during as Britain has proposed.

It appeared to dash hopes raised by some politicians that the IRA might declare a new ceasefire after the Protestant "marching season", which reached a relatively peaceful climax on Saturday, the order's cherished "Glorious 12th of July".

Adams' statement followed appeals by Britain's new Labour government for an end to the Irish Republican Army's (IRA) war against British rule which would earn Sinn Fein a seat at the peace talks within six weeks if it was genuine.
"If people want us to persuade the IRA to end its campaign...then they need to be giving us the ability to do that," Adams said.

He said that although Britain was no longer demanding that the IRA disarm to earn Sinn Fein a seat at the talks, proposals that it surrender weapons during the talks "retains the potential to block progress during negotiations".
The head of Northern Ireland's biggest pro-British group, the Ulster Unionist party, said on Sunday that talk of an IRA truce was "wishful thinking".
"The reality is that Sinn Fein/IRA are committed to violence in order to achieve objectives that no democrat can support," Trimble said.

Trimble said Britain should abandon hopes of involving Sinn Fein in the talks, which resume on Tuesday after some of the worst rioting the province has seen and a landmark climbdown by the Orange Order over its annual marches.

"What the (British) Prime Minister and the government are trying to do only makes sense on the basis of leaving Sinn fein behind, and consequently for the democratic parties to be discussing among themselves," he said.

He recalled that the IRA injured five members of the security forces in a North Belfast ambush on the eve of the 12th of July when the Orange Order recalls a 1690 Protestant victory over a Catholic king with province-wide marches.
The order scrapped four flashpoint parades under the threat of mass counter demonstrations by Catholics who call them intimidation but went ahead with hundreds of others on Saturday.
Moderate Catholic nationlist leader John Hume hailed the "moral courge"" of the Orange Order for defusing fears of sectarian strife by calling off marches.
Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), urged all sides to seize a chance for progress.

"Let us now move forward from the constructive decisions by the Orange Order and build upon that, and let's work to keep building that new atmosphere in order to create an agreed society for the first time," Hume said on BBC television.
Police said Northern Ireland was calm after tension that soared one week ago when Britain allowed an Orange Order parade along the Catholic Garvaghy Road of Portadown.
They reported clashes with Catholics in Londonderry overnight when youths attacked police with stones, petrol-bombs and catapults firing ball-bearings.
